html:
The Shona are the largest people of Zimbabwe, Bantu-speaking farmers and cattle keepers of the high plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers. The map shows Shona lands in 1880 and 1900.

Their ancestors built Great Zimbabwe and later states such as Mutapa and the Rozvi kingdom, which traded gold and ivory to the Indian Ocean coast. By the 1800s these had broken up into many chiefdoms. In the west they were raided by the Ndebele kingdom.

In 1890 Cecil Rhodes's Pioneer Column marched onto the plateau and founded Fort Salisbury, today's Harare. The British South Africa Company took land and cattle and forced people to work. In 1896 the Shona rose together with the Ndebele, in the uprising Zimbabweans call the First Chimurenga. Spirit mediums such as Mbuya Nehanda helped lead it; she was hanged in 1898 and became a symbol for the later liberation war.
